speakerTitle: Consultant in Diabetes & Endocrinology and Medication Safety Lead
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Diabetes & Endocrine Unit
speakerBio: Endocrinologist and trust medication-safety lead who has spent a decade chasing the letter 'U' off drug charts and teaching foundation doctors that insulin is the friendliest drug in medicine right up until it is the deadliest.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

It is 02:10. A ward nurse bleeps you: a 78-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia, on a variable-rate insulin infusion earlier, now has a capillary glucose of 1.6 mmol/L and is unrousable. You pull the drug chart. Six hours ago a locum wrote "Novorapid 6U" — but the "U" was tight against the number, and the ward received it as "60". She got sixty units of rapid-acting insulin subcutaneously. This is not a pharmacology curiosity. Insulin is the drug that most often kills people by a decimal point, and tonight the decimal point was a badly-formed letter. We are going to make sure you never write that "U".

1 · 💉 Why insulin is different — the physiology you are replacing

Every rational insulin regimen is an attempt to mimic what a working pancreas does. The healthy beta-cell secretes insulin in two patterns, and understanding them is the whole game:

  • Basal secretion — a low, continuous trickle (roughly 0.5–1 unit/hour) that runs 24 hours a day. Its job is to restrain hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight, and — critically in type 1 — to suppress ketogenesis. Without basal insulin the liver runs unchecked: gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and unrestrained lipolysis pour glucose and ketones into the blood.
  • Prandial (bolus) secretion — a sharp spike released within minutes of eating, matched to the carbohydrate load, that disposes of the post-meal glucose surge into muscle and fat.
Basal insulin keeps you alive between meals; bolus insulin gets you through a meal. Take away the basal in a type 1 and ketosis begins within hours — a person with type 1 diabetes always needs background insulin, even when nil-by-mouth, even when not eating.
💡 The mimicry principle

Basal-bolus (a long-acting insulin once or twice daily + rapid-acting insulin with each meal) is the regimen that most closely reproduces normal physiology, which is why it is the default for type 1 diabetes and for many unwell inpatients. Everything else — premixed twice-daily, sliding scales — is a compromise on this ideal, and you should be able to say what it trades away.

2 · ⏱️ The insulin families and their time-action profiles

You cannot prescribe insulin safely without a mental picture of onset, peak and duration for each class. The peak is where hypoglycaemia lives; the duration is where the overlap traps are. Learn this table cold.

ClassExamplesOnsetPeakDurationRole
Ultra-rapidFiasp (faster aspart), Lyumjev (ultra-rapid lispro)~2–5 min~1 h3–5 hPrandial; closest to a physiological meal spike, can dose at start of meal
Rapid-acting analogueAspart (NovoRapid), lispro (Humalog), glulisine (Apidra)~10–20 min~1–2 h3–5 hPrandial bolus; give with/just before food
Short-acting (soluble/regular)Actrapid, Humulin S, Regular~30–60 min~2–4 h~6–8 hThe insulin used IV; prandial if given ~30 min before food
Intermediate (isophane/NPH)Insulatard, Humulin I, Insuman Basal~1–2 h~4–8 h~12–16 hBasal (twice daily); the pronounced peak is a hypo risk, esp. nocturnal
Long-acting analogueGlargine U100 (Lantus), detemir (Levemir)~1–2 hMinimal / flat~18–24 hBasal, once (or twice) daily; flatter than NPH → fewer nocturnal hypos
Ultra-long-actingGlargine U300 (Toujeo), degludec (Tresiba)~1–6 hFlat>24–42 hVery stable basal; degludec's long tail is forgiving of variable timing but slow to titrate
Premixed (biphasic)NovoMix 30, Humulin M3, Humalog Mix25/50Rapid + intermediate combinedTwo peaks~12–16 hTwice-daily convenience; fixed ratio removes flexibility, more hypos
🎯 Reading the number in the name

The number in a premix is the percentage of rapid-acting component: NovoMix 30 = 30% aspart / 70% protaminated (intermediate) aspart. Humalog Mix25 = 25% lispro. Higher first number = bigger prandial punch and bigger early-peak hypo risk.

3 · 🧪 Concentrated insulins — where the maths kills

Standard insulin is U-100: 100 units per mL. To reduce injection volume in insulin-resistant or high-dose patients, manufacturers make concentrated formulations. Each is a documented source of ten- and five-fold errors.

ProductConcentrationThe trap
U-100 (default)100 units/mLThe reference. Every U-100 syringe is calibrated to this.
Glargine U-300 (Toujeo)300 units/mLOnly ever dispensed in its own pen — never withdraw into a syringe. Dial units, not mL. Not interchangeable unit-for-unit with U-100 glargine.
Lispro/aspart U-200 (Humalog 200, Lyumjev 200)200 units/mLPen-only, dial in units. Danger if withdrawn into a U-100 syringe → double dose.
Regular U-500 (Humulin R U-500)500 units/mLThe most dangerous vial on the ward. Five times concentrated. Has BOTH bolus and basal action. Must be prescribed in units with the concentration stated, ideally with a dedicated U-500 syringe. A U-100 syringe drawn to "20" delivers 100 units.
⚠️ The U-500 syringe trap

If a U-500 vial is drawn up with an ordinary U-100 insulin syringe, every mark delivers five times the labelled units. Institutions that stock U-500 must dispense a dedicated U-500 syringe or a U-500 pen, and the prescription must always state both the number of units and the product's concentration. If you are ever handed a U-500 vial and a U-100 syringe, stop and call pharmacy.

4 · 🚫 Insulin as a 'Never Event' medication — the classic errors

Insulin sits at the top of every "high-alert medication" list precisely because small slips have large consequences and it is administered thousands of times a day. The recurring, patterned errors — memorise them, because each has a specific defence:

ErrorMechanismThe defence
"U" or "IU" misread"10U" read as "100"; "IU" read as "10". A tenfold overdose from one letter.Always write the word "units" in full. Never abbreviate to U or IU. This is a hard national standard.
Wrong insulin productBasal charted where bolus was meant (e.g. Lantus vs NovoRapid), or a premix swapped for a basal.Prescribe by full brand name + device; check basal vs bolus role at every round.
Look-alike / sound-alike namesHumalog vs Humulin; NovoRapid vs NovoMix; Lantus vs Levemir; Toujeo vs Lantus.Independent double-check of the exact product against the chart before drawing up.
IV vs SC confusionAn IV-intended dose given SC (or vice versa); wrong-route with a giant concentration mismatch.Only soluble/short-acting (or rapid analogue in fixed protocols) insulin goes IV; never give long-acting analogues IV. State the route explicitly.
Pump failure → DKAAn insulin pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin. If it fails, there is no basal depot — ketosis and DKA follow within hours.Recognise a pump; have a backup basal plan; check ketones early in any unwell pump patient.
Sliding scale without basalPrescribing only correction doses reactively, with no background insulin — glucose rollercoasters and, in type 1, ketosis.Never manage a type 1 on "sliding scale alone"; continue basal always.
Withholding for "nil by mouth"All insulin stopped when a type 1 is fasted for theatre → DKA on the trolley.Basal continues (often reduced); use a variable-rate IV insulin infusion for prolonged fasting.
Write the word "units" every single time. The three most expensive characters in medicine are the ones you saved by writing "U".

5 · ✅ Safe-prescribing rules and double-checks

Turn the errors above into a checklist you run on every insulin prescription:

  1. Write "units" in full — never U, never IU, never "iu".
  2. Name the exact product and device — brand, concentration, pen or vial. "Insulin 10 units" is not a safe order.
  3. State the route — SC or IV. Only soluble/short-acting insulin (or protocol rapid analogue) goes IV.
  4. Independent double-check — a second competent person verifies product, dose, concentration and route before administration, especially for IV infusions and any concentrated insulin.
  5. Link boluses to meals — prescribe prandial doses "with breakfast/lunch/dinner", not rigid clock times, if the patient's eating is erratic.
  6. Reconcile the patient's own regimen on admission — most inpatient insulin harm comes from disrupting a regimen the patient managed perfectly at home. Where safe, let stable self-managing patients keep control (self-administration).
  7. Prescribe hypo rescue proactively — every insulin-treated inpatient should have a hypoglycaemia treatment protocol available on the chart.
💡 The insulin passport / prescription chart

Insulin-specific prescription charts (separate from the general drug chart, forcing "units" to be written and product/device to be documented) measurably reduce error. If your trust has an insulin chart, use it — the design is doing safety work for you.

6 · 🔁 Insulin pump therapy — the basics and the DKA landmine

A continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin: a programmed basal rate through the day plus patient-triggered meal boluses. There is no long-acting depot anywhere in the body. This is the single most important fact about a pump patient on your ward.

⚠️ Pump failure = no basal = rapid DKA

Because the only insulin on board is rapid-acting with a 3–5 hour duration, any interruption — a kinked cannula, a failed set, an empty reservoir, a dislodged infusion site, the pump switched off for a scan — removes all basal insulin within hours. A type 1 on a pump can be in ketosis within 4–6 hours and DKA soon after, even with a normal or only mildly raised glucose. If a pump patient is unwell, vomiting, or hyperglycaemic: check ketones immediately, do not assume the pump is working, and be ready to give SC rapid-acting insulin by pen/syringe or start a variable-rate IV insulin infusion.

  • On admission: document that the patient uses a pump, the insulin type, and their basal rates. Wherever the patient is competent and well, let them keep self-managing — they know their pump far better than the ward.
  • Sick-day rule for pumps: if ketones rise or the pump is suspect, fall back to injections (basal + bolus by pen) and treat as any unwell type 1.
  • Going to theatre/imaging: agree a plan with the diabetes team — many pumps must come off for MRI/CT, and a bridging IV insulin infusion is then mandatory.

7 · 📋 Master insulin profile — the one-page reference

NeedReach forBecause
Cover a mealRapid analogue (aspart/lispro/glulisine) or ultra-rapid (Fiasp/Lyumjev)Fast on, short off — matches the post-meal spike, minimal tail into the next gap
Flat 24-h backgroundLong/ultra-long analogue (glargine, detemir, degludec)Peakless → fewer nocturnal hypos than NPH
IV infusion (DKA/HHS/perioperative)Soluble/short-acting (Actrapid) — never a long-acting analogueShort half-life gives minute-to-minute control; long-acting IV would stack dangerously
Twice-daily convenience, eats regularlyPremixed biphasic (NovoMix 30, Humulin M3)One pen does prandial + basal — at the cost of flexibility and more hypos
Severe insulin resistance / very high dosesConcentrated (U-200, U-300, U-500) — pen/dedicated syringe onlySmaller volume — but a five/two/three-fold concentration trap; prescribe in units + state concentration
Type 1, any settingBasal-bolus (never basal-free)Mimics physiology and keeps ketogenesis suppressed even when not eating
☠️ M&M — the tenfold overdose written in one letter

A 78-year-old woman was admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Her usual home regimen was NovoRapid 6 units with meals. Overnight a tired locum, writing quickly on the general drug chart, put "NovoRapid 6U" — but the loop of the 6 ran into the U, and the U itself looked like a trailing zero. The night nurse, cross-checking against a glucose of 14, read the order as "60" and, seeing a high sugar, felt it plausible. Sixty units of rapid-acting insulin went in subcutaneously at 20:00. By 02:00 she was unrousable with a glucose of 1.6 mmol/L; the SC depot meant the hypoglycaemia was deep and prolonged, requiring repeated IV glucose and a 10% infusion over many hours, and she suffered an aspiration event during the episode. Root causes: the abbreviation "U" (never write it — write "units"); prescribing on a general chart rather than an insulin chart that forces the word; no independent double-check for a high-alert drug; and anchoring bias ("sugar was high, so a big dose seemed right"). Every defence that failed was a system defence we teach in this session. She survived; the next patient might not.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Insulin replaces two physiological patterns — basal (keeps ketosis away, runs even when NBM) and bolus (covers meals). Basal-bolus mimics the body.
  2. Know the time-action profiles — rapid/ultra-rapid for meals, long/ultra-long for background, soluble for IV. The peak is where the hypo lives.
  3. Write "units" in full — never U or IU. This single habit prevents the classic tenfold error.
  4. Concentrated insulins (U-200/U-300/U-500) are pen/dedicated-syringe only; state the concentration and dose in units.
  5. Insulin is a Never-Event drug: guard against wrong product, look-alike names, IV/SC confusion, and sliding-scale-without-basal with named product, route, and an independent double-check.
  6. A pump delivers only rapid insulin — pump failure means no basal depot and DKA within hours. Check ketones early in any unwell pump patient.
  7. Never stop basal insulin in a type 1, even fasting — bridge with a variable-rate IV insulin infusion.

moderatorQs.q: A type 1 patient is being made nil-by-mouth for morning theatre. The house officer suggests holding all their insulin overnight. Why is that dangerous, and what do you do instead?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because a person with type 1 diabetes has no endogenous insulin, and basal insulin is what suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and, crucially, ketogenesis. Stop it and they will develop ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis within hours — you can arrive at the anaesthetic room with a fasted, ketotic patient. The rule is never stop basal insulin in a type 1. For a short fast you continue the usual basal (often at a modestly reduced dose) and omit only the prandial boluses; for prolonged fasting or major surgery you start a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII) with concurrent glucose substrate and monitor glucose and ketones. The principle is that these patients always need background insulin, eating or not.

moderatorQs.q: Walk us through exactly why an insulin pump patient can be in DKA with only a modestly raised glucose within a few hours of a device problem.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A CSII pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin — there is no long-acting subcutaneous depot anywhere in the body. The programmed basal rate is a continuous micro-infusion of insulin with a duration of only 3–5 hours. If the cannula kinks, the set fails, the site dislodges or the pump is switched off, all basal insulin ceases and the remaining insulin is gone within a few hours. Without basal insulin the liver ramps up lipolysis and ketogenesis, so ketosis and acidosis develop before the glucose has time to climb dramatically — the patient can be ketotic and acidotic with a glucose that looks only moderately high. That is why in any unwell or vomiting pump patient you check ketones immediately, assume the pump may have failed, and fall back to injected insulin or a VRIII rather than trusting the device.

moderatorQs.q: What is it specifically about the abbreviations 'U' and 'IU' that makes them a national never-write standard, and what is the safer alternative?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The letter 'U' written after a number is repeatedly misread as a trailing zero, turning 10 into 100 — a tenfold overdose — and 'IU' (international units) is misread as '10' or 'IO', inflating the dose again. Because insulin has a narrow therapeutic margin and is dosed in small numbers where one extra zero is catastrophic, this is one of the highest-yield error patterns in medicine. The universal safe practice is to write the word 'units' in full every single time, name the exact product and device, and prescribe on an insulin-specific chart that structurally forces this. It costs three characters and prevents a tenfold overdose.

audienceQs.q: I'm handed a vial labelled U-500 and an ordinary insulin syringe to give '20 units'. What do I do?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Stop — do not draw it up with that syringe. An ordinary insulin syringe is calibrated for U-100; a U-500 vial is five times as concentrated, so every mark on a U-100 syringe delivers five times the labelled units — drawing to '20' would give 100 units, a potentially fatal dose. U-500 must be given with a dedicated U-500 syringe or a U-500 pen, and the prescription must state the number of units and the concentration. Call pharmacy, confirm the intended dose in units, and get the correct device before anything goes into the patient.

audienceQs.q: A patient's chart says 'Humalog 30 units twice daily' as their basal. Something feels off — how do I catch this class of error?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Your instinct is right: Humalog is a rapid-acting bolus insulin, not a basal, and the twice-daily basal role plus the look-alike name suggests a Humalog vs Humalog Mix vs Humulin I mix-up. This is a classic look-alike/sound-alike and wrong-role error. Verify against the patient's own regimen or GP record, clarify whether they meant Humalog Mix25/50 (a premix) or Humulin I (isophane basal), and confirm the exact product, concentration and device directly with the prescriber before it is given. Systematically, prescribing by full brand name and checking basal-vs-bolus role at every drug round catches this pattern.

audienceQs.q: A well type 1 patient who manages their own basal-bolus wants to keep controlling their insulin on the ward. Is that safe?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Usually yes, and it is often safer than handing control to a busy ward team unfamiliar with their regimen — most inpatient insulin harm comes from disrupting a regimen the patient ran perfectly at home. Use your trust's insulin self-administration risk assessment: confirm the patient is cognitively able, not acutely confused or critically unwell, can safely store and access their insulin, and agree that they will document doses and report hypos. The prescription still appears on the chart and glucose is still monitored, but the patient administers. Reassess if their condition deteriorates, and always keep a hypoglycaemia rescue protocol available.
